segments.description: Welcome to the Australian Open Global Coaches Conference 2026 with the main topic from the Orange Court to World Class presented by Kai Gerber, Germany. On this slide, I want to give you some insights to my personal coaching career and what I'm doing right now at this moment. So first of all, I'm an owner and a head coach of our own tennis academy in Basel, Switzerland. On the other side, you see the brand of our international kids tennis and youth coaching conference, which we host since 2018 in Basel, Switzerland, and since 2023 in an engagement with the ATP 500 Tournament Swiss Indoor. And the third pillar I work in is in our sports management agency, where we take care on young athletes, bringing big brands to the ATP and WTA Tour or organize smaller business events for our customers. With my today's presentation, I want to show the audience absolutely how important it is to build a big and bright foundation in the early ages in youth tennis development. The Orange Court, the intermediate development stage in kids tennis between red and green is a crucial yet often underestimated step in the education of young tennis players. Also, it plays a key pedagogical and developmental role. It receives too little attention in many countries and federations. The reasons lie in a combination of structural, cultural and educational factors. It's a lack of understanding of the development process.

Many coaches, parents and officials mistakenly see the Orange Court merely as a transition phase rather than an essential development platform. In reality, this stage is a critical for technical optimization, tactical awareness and movement intelligence. Children learn to read the court, understand angles and develop their first offensive strategies, skills that are difficult to acquire later. This lack of understanding often leads to the premature skipping of the Orange stage in effort to reach full court faster. The pressure for early results and misguided success criteria, a widespread issue is early focus on results and rankings. Parents and clubs often want quick, visible success and measure progress by tournament wins instead of learning progress. As a result, children are frequently pushed too early onto the green court or full court at the expense of technical quality, tactical understanding and enjoyment. The green court thus becomes a victim of short-term thinking, undermines long-term development. The problem of the race to the yellow ball and why it's problematic. By a mechanical overload, the yellow ball bounces higher and moves faster. Children compensate with unnatural movements and poor technique. The tactical limitations on the full court, children lose their sense of space, angles and variation making their play one dimensional. Third, the loss of enjoyment. When children are over challenged, they lose motivation and confidence.

At point number four, there's a lack of sustainability. Early success with a yellow ball really leads to long-term performance development. In short playing, yellow too soon means learning less, not more. Before Orange players advanced to the 78 green format, based on this video provided, we can clearly see what it truly means to train children effectively on the Orange court. With care, structure, long-term vision, the goal is not only to teach them how to play but prepare them mentally, technically and physically for the next stages of the tennis journey. From the Orange court to the line court and cream-up building, the players should understand net coverage, which is dependent upon the placement and quality of their approach shot. The players should have the ability to flatten out balls that are short and high and holding serve is an achievable goal. These two players are ready to begin the transition to the 78 green format. So here's my take-home messages for all attendees from my perspective. The value of the Orange court in children's tennis. First, the age-appropriate environment. The smaller court size and lower compromising, balls slow the game down, allowing children to experience success earlier and develop proper technique without physical strain. Second, the technical learning with quality. The Orange court enables players to execute full strokes with correct biomechanics.

It supports the development of stable grips, controlled swing path, and balanced movement patterns. Third, the tactical awareness and decision-making. Because rallies last longer, players can begin to understand when and why use certain shots. They learn to construct points, recognize space, and think strategically. Number four, the footwork and the coordination. The reduced court dimensions encourage dynamic movement, rhythm, and coordination. Essential building blocks for later performance on full-size courts. Number five, the psychological and emotional growth. The Orange stage promotes confidence, focus, and resilience. It allows children to experience competition in a manageable context, emphasizing learning and enjoyment over results. Six, the social interaction and team spirit. The format forces communication, cooperation, respect among players, key values in both and personal development. Number seven, the smooth transition to the green and full court later on. The progression from orange to green ensures contingency. Players learn here timing, spacing, and tactical structure, transfer naturally to the next level. As my friend and mentor, Michael Eppert, so beautiful says, this concept aims at a fast development of tactical and technical skills in tennis, and also at making this sport more fun to play for children and for life. In the two short side-by-side videos we can already observe on the Orange court the same

tactical patterns that later appear at the work-class level. This clearly demonstrates the fundamental principles of high performance tennis can and should be introduced at an early stage, provided the training environment is developmentally accurate. Three technical parallels between the Orange court and elite tennis. First, use of spacing angles, second, rally construction and point patterns, and defense recovery and counterplay. At this point I would like to express my deep gratitude to Michael Eppert from Austria for his outstanding collaboration and invaluable contributions. His pioneering work and scientific research have played a decisive role in shaping the foundation of modern-use tennis development. As a founder of the Orange and Lime Courts concept for the ITF in the early 2000s, Michi helped establish a global framework that continues to influence how children learn and experience the game today. Michi's contributions to modern tennis development. Scientific foundation of scaled courts. Michi's research provided the imperial basics of adapting court-sized ball compromises and racket specifications to children's physical and cognitive development. This ensured that learning tennis became more natural, enjoyable and biomechanically sound. The introduction of the Orange and Lime Court system. His concept bridged the gap between red and green stages, creating a smoother developmentally

aligned progression that allowed players to build tactical and tactical skills systematically. The collaboration with the ITF. Through his work with the International Tennis Federation he had standardised the global play and stay philosophy, which remains a commonstone of junior tennis programs worldwide. It's a data-driven coaching and research. Michi's approach culminated practical coaching insights with scientific evidence, emphasising measurable progress and long-term athlete development rather than early specification. This key message means long-term development over early success. It's not about being great at 12, early performance says little about long-term potential. What truly matters is continuous, joyful improvements step by step, year by year. The preventing dropout. When training becomes too intense, too serious or too result-orientated, too early, many children lose their love to the game. Our mission is to keep every child in the sport inspired and motivated to grow, to protecting the body. Overloading young bodies can cause injuries and long-term physical issues. Children must respect each children's development stage, emphasising proper technique, coordination and recovery. Building a lifelong passion. Tennis should be a source of fun, friendship and self-confidence. When children enjoy the process, they naturally develop a consistent and healthy competitive

spirit. A sustainable player development, a slow, through-fall progression ensures that physical, technical and emotional growth stay in balance, creating players who are resilient, skilled and love the game for life. To support and validate my observations, I also reached out to my long-term friend and mentor, Oymud Sorvald, from Norway, whose expertise and experience bring valuable perspective. Oymud works closely with Casper Ruth, one of the most successful players in Norwegian tennis history, as well as Nikolai Butkovkir, one of Norway's most promising young talents. His inside bridge, the gap between grassroot development and elite performance, illustrating how the same principles apply across all levels. Please listen to him and his insights. For me personally, this is one of the most inspiring examples seeing Emma Raducano first on the Orange Court. As a young player and then 10 years later lifting the US Open trophy, this visual journey perfectly illustrates how early developmental work, when done with purpose and understanding, can evolve into world-class performance. The continuity of development from Orange Court to the US Open Champion, early tactical awareness. Even as a child, Emma displayed a clear sense of structure in her rallies, building points using space intelligently and burying tempo. These same tactical foundations are visible in her professional matches.

The technical precision and adaptability, her continuity and ability to adjust to different situations steamed from years of balanced training that valued both from the mental composure and competitive mindset. The calm focus, the manner she showed at the US Open was not accidental, it was cultivated with years of process-orientated development, where learning and resilience were prioritized over early results. The game identity, the way she steps today, proactive, intelligent and composed, reflects a long-term development philosophy that began on smaller courts with big ideas. In my conclusion, I would like to show you five pillars. The Orange Court offers the opportunity to develop skills and early age that are absolutely essential in performance tennis. Second, if we want to improve the quality of training at young age, the Orange Court is the first choice and far more than just a nice to have. Three, we need to spend more time training on the Orange Court and link the training period not to the player's age, but to their playing level. Number four, coaches, parents and players, especially children, must be convinced of the advantage of the Orange Court. Number five, the training concept and the competition system must be aligned at all. I would also like to highlight my collaboration with WADA, a partnership that adds an essential dimension to our holistic approach in players' development.

Together, we focus on the mental and emotional aspects of coaching, ensuring that both coaches and parents are equipped with the tools to support young athletes effectively and sustainable. Con the collaboration with WADA, mental coaching for coaches and parents, focus on mental strength and emotional intelligence. The program embraces the importance of self-awareness, communication and emotional regulation, key factors that influence both coaching quality and player well-being. The support for coaches, WADA provides structured guidance on how to create a positive learning, environment manager pressure, situations and foster intrinsic motivation in players. The support to the parents, parents receive insights on how a company, the Children's Tennis Journey, constructively balancing encouragement with patients and understanding the developmental process behind performance. The access via QR code, by scanning the QR code provided, you will be directed to a dedicated page offering resources, articles and practical tools on mental coaching for coaches and parents. This platform serves a bridge between scientific understanding and everyday practice. At this point, I would like to express my sincere gratitude for the invitation to be a speaker and to thank everyone involved for this wonderful opportunity. It is a true honor to be part of this year's Coaches Conference, surrounded by so many

passionate and dedicated professionals who share the same vision for the future of tennis. My message and application and inspiration, gratitude and honor being invited to contribute as a speaker among such an inspiring group of coaches is both humbling and motivating. The exchange of ideas, experiences and perspectives is what drives our sport absolutely forward. Conference like this reminds us that coaching is more than teaching technique, it's about shaping people, nurturing potential and building a culture of growth and respect. To all participants, I wish you an enriching and joyful experience. Ladies events spark new connections, insights and inspiration that continue to resonate long after the conference. All the best from Germany, Kai.
